<Rep. Danny K. Davis>: Child support is one of our most cost-effective tools to reduce child poverty, collecting more than four dollars for every dollar we invest. The child support program increases access to basic necessities for children who would otherwise live in deep poverty. I strongly support real-world reforms to the child support program that center all decision-making on the child's well-being. I strongly support collecting current and past-due child support; however, I oppose this bill based on numerous concerns.
Current law already gives flexibility to the Secretary of State to limit, restrict, or revoke one's passport if states determine that step is needed and effective. In contrast, this bill removes judgement and consideration of circumstances by mandating revocation while excluding any lesser option that may be more appropriate, like limiting the passport. This inflexibility promises to impose hardship and create large implementation challenges while doing very little to improve child support collections. Our colleagues on the House Foreign Affairs Committee also raised concerns about this bill.
Despite its name--Ensuring Children Receive Support Act, this bill does absolutely nothing to ensure that states pass through all child support to the families. Because of federal limits and states not using options in the law, dozens of states actually keep large amounts of child support rather than giving it to custodial parents, which reduces support to families. This bill could have lived up to its name and required states to give all child support to the children, but it did not.
Rather, this bill continues the same, age-old, punitive child support policy approaches that typically and disproportionally harm lower-income families that will not ensure noncustodial parents adhere to their orders. If revoking a passport is the most effective approach to collecting child support, current law already allows the state and federal government to do so--and they should. However, mandating a likely-ineffective, harsh approach while inaccurately proclaiming to ensure children get the financial support they deserve rings hollow.
Our Committee has clear, specific opportunities to improve federal child support programs to ensure children's needs are met, families are strengthened, and both custodial and noncustodial parents are treated fairly.
States should pass through all child support to the families. I am proud of Illinois' leadership in this area, which is making a meaningful difference for the people I represent.
We should prohibit states from collecting child support from families whose children enter foster care. The research is abundantly clear that this punitive action keeps children in foster care longer. Although more states are stopping this practice after the Department of Health and Human Service issued guidance, this Committee should act to stop this process.
We should legislate based on reality and not on the longstanding fictional narrative that noncustodial parents do not want to pay child support. Most noncustodial parents struggling with child support lack good jobs that allow them to pay without being forced into poverty, and they are reluctant to use their limited income to pay support that is not given to their children.
We should move bills that encourage the right-sizing of child support orders, investment in employment and economic upscaling opportunities for struggling noncustodial parents, in parenting time services, and funding parental access and visitation grants that help address parental conflict and require evidence-based protocols to ensure that parenting time is not a weapon for perpetrators of domestic violence.
We have found common ground on positive, effective child support policies before, and I hope we will prioritize these reforms again.
Danny K. Davis,
Member of Congress.
